courses.title: Psychiatry
courses.description: Psychiatric assessment, psychotic and mood disorders, anxiety disorders, substance use, child and adolescent psychiatry, and mental health law and services in Nigeria.

topics.title: Psychiatric Assessment and Mental Health in Nigeria
topics.summary: History, mental state examination, risk assessment, and the context of mental health care.

material.heading: Assessment
material.body: Psychiatric assessment includes the presenting complaint, history of present illness, past psychiatric and medical history, drug and substance history, family history, personal history (birth, development, education, occupation, relationships, forensic history) and premorbid personality. The mental state examination (MSE) records: appearance and behaviour; speech (rate, volume, flow — pressure of speech in mania); mood (subjective) and affect (objective — blunted, incongruent); thought form (flight of ideas, loosening of associations, thought block) and content (delusions — fixed false beliefs not in keeping with cultural background; overvalued ideas; obsessions; suicidal ideation); perception (hallucinations — perception without a stimulus; illusions); cognition (orientation, attention, memory — MMSE); and insight. Risk assessment covers suicide, self-harm, harm to others and self-neglect. Cultural context matters: beliefs about spiritual causes are common, so distinguishing culturally shared beliefs from delusions is essential.
keyPoints: Delusion: fixed false belief not culturally shared

material.heading: Context in Nigeria
material.body: Mental disorders are common (depression, anxiety, psychosis, substance use), yet there are very few psychiatrists (about 300 for over 200 million people) and most care is delivered in federal neuropsychiatric hospitals (e.g. Yaba, Aro Abeokuta) and by traditional and faith healers, where chaining and other human rights abuses can occur. Stigma is widespread. The treatment gap exceeds 80%. The WHO mhGAP Intervention Guide supports non-specialist health workers to manage priority conditions in primary care (task-sharing). The National Mental Health Act 2021 (replacing the colonial Lunacy Act of 1958) promotes rights-based care, community services, voluntary admission and safeguards for involuntary admission. Attempted suicide was historically criminalised under the Criminal Code; advocacy seeks decriminalisation. Common psychosocial stressors include poverty, insecurity (insurgency, kidnapping), displacement and substance use.
keyPoints: National Mental Health Act 2021 (replaced Lunacy Act 1958)
Human rights abuses in some healing homes

topics.title: Schizophrenia and Psychotic Disorders
topics.summary: Features, diagnosis, antipsychotic treatment and substance-induced psychosis.

material.heading: Schizophrenia
material.body: Schizophrenia (lifetime prevalence ~1%) usually begins in late adolescence or early adulthood. Positive symptoms: delusions (persecutory, reference, control), hallucinations (third-person auditory hallucinations — running commentary, voices discussing the patient), thought disorder and Schneider's first-rank symptoms (thought insertion, withdrawal, broadcasting, passivity experiences). Negative symptoms: blunted affect, alogia, avolition, social withdrawal and anhedonia. Cognitive deficits affect functioning. Diagnosis requires symptoms for at least 1 month (ICD-11) with exclusion of organic causes (drugs, delirium, epilepsy, HIV, neurosyphilis, thyroid disease). Differentials: brief psychotic disorder (acute and transient, common in Africa with good prognosis), schizoaffective and bipolar disorder, and substance-induced psychosis (cannabis — 'Indian hemp' — tramadol, methamphetamine 'mkpuru mmiri' in south-eastern Nigeria). Good prognostic factors: acute onset, clear precipitant, older onset, female sex, mood symptoms, good premorbid functioning and family support.

material.heading: Treatment
material.body: Antipsychotics are the mainstay: first-generation (haloperidol, chlorpromazine, fluphenazine decanoate depot — widely used in Nigeria; extrapyramidal side effects — acute dystonia, akathisia, parkinsonism, tardive dyskinesia; hyperprolactinaemia) and second-generation (risperidone, olanzapine — weight gain, diabetes, dyslipidaemia; clozapine for treatment-resistant schizophrenia after two failed trials — agranulocytosis monitoring). Long-acting injectable depots help adherence. Neuroleptic malignant syndrome (fever, rigidity, autonomic instability, confusion, raised CK) is an emergency — stop antipsychotic, supportive care, dantrolene/bromocriptine. Psychosocial interventions: psychoeducation for patient and family, family therapy (reducing high expressed emotion), cognitive behavioural therapy for psychosis, social skills training, supported employment and community rehabilitation. Acute agitation: calm de-escalation, then oral or IM haloperidol plus promethazine or a benzodiazepine.

topics.title: Mood and Anxiety Disorders
topics.summary: Depression, bipolar disorder, suicide, anxiety and trauma-related disorders.

material.heading: Mood disorders
material.body: Depression: persistent low mood, loss of interest or pleasure (anhedonia), fatigue, sleep and appetite change, poor concentration, guilt, psychomotor change and suicidal thoughts for at least 2 weeks. In Nigeria, depression often presents with somatic complaints ('heat in the head', crawling sensations, body pains). Screen with PHQ-9. Treatment: psychoeducation, psychological therapies (CBT, problem-solving therapy, interpersonal therapy — deliverable by trained lay workers, e.g. the Friendship Bench model), and antidepressants (SSRIs — fluoxetine, sertraline; amitriptyline widely available but toxic in overdose); ECT for severe or psychotic depression. Bipolar disorder: episodes of mania (elevated or irritable mood, reduced need for sleep, grandiosity, pressured speech, flight of ideas, risky behaviour, lasting ≥ 1 week) and depression; treat mania with antipsychotics and mood stabilisers (lithium — narrow therapeutic range, monitor levels, renal and thyroid function; valproate — avoid in women of childbearing potential; carbamazepine). Suicide risk factors: previous attempt, depression, substance use, hopelessness, chronic illness, male sex, social isolation; pesticide ingestion is a common method in Nigeria.

material.heading: Anxiety and trauma
material.body: Generalised anxiety disorder (excessive worry ≥ 6 months with muscle tension, restlessness, poor sleep), panic disorder (recurrent unexpected panic attacks with fear of further attacks), phobias (social, specific, agoraphobia) and obsessive–compulsive disorder (obsessions and compulsions — SSRIs and exposure and response prevention). Post-traumatic stress disorder follows traumatic events (insurgency in the north-east, kidnapping, banditry, sexual violence, road crashes): re-experiencing (flashbacks, nightmares), avoidance, negative mood and hyperarousal for more than a month; treated with trauma-focused CBT or EMDR, and SSRIs. Acute stress reactions and adjustment disorders are common after disasters; psychological first aid supports affected communities. Treatment of anxiety disorders: CBT, SSRIs; avoid long-term benzodiazepines (dependence).

topics.title: Substance Use Disorders
topics.summary: Alcohol, cannabis, opioids (tramadol, codeine), stimulants, withdrawal and management.

material.heading: Patterns and assessment
material.body: Nigeria's National Drug Use Survey (2018) found about 14% of adults (14.3 million) used drugs other than alcohol and tobacco in the past year — mainly cannabis, followed by non-medical use of prescription opioids (tramadol, codeine cough syrup), cough syrups and sedatives, with rising methamphetamine and inhalant use; alcohol (including local brews such as ogogoro and burukutu) is widely used. Dependence (ICD-11) involves impaired control, increasing priority over other activities, and physiological features (tolerance, withdrawal). Screening tools: AUDIT for alcohol, ASSIST for other substances, CAGE. Complications: psychosis, depression, suicide, accidents, violence, liver disease (alcohol), HIV and hepatitis (injecting), seizures (tramadol toxicity), and social harms. Brief interventions using motivational interviewing are effective in primary care.

material.heading: Withdrawal and treatment
material.body: Alcohol withdrawal begins 6–24 hours after the last drink: tremor, sweating, anxiety, tachycardia; seizures (12–48 hours); delirium tremens (48–72 hours — confusion, hallucinations, autonomic instability; potentially fatal). Treat with benzodiazepines (chlordiazepoxide or diazepam — reducing regimen) and thiamine (IV Pabrinex before glucose to prevent Wernicke's encephalopathy — confusion, ataxia, ophthalmoplegia; untreated can lead to Korsakoff's syndrome with amnesia and confabulation). Relapse prevention: acamprosate, naltrexone, disulfiram, psychosocial support, Alcoholics Anonymous. Opioid withdrawal (yawning, rhinorrhoea, dilated pupils, piloerection, diarrhoea, cramps) is unpleasant but rarely dangerous; opioid agonist treatment (methadone — introduced in Nigeria in 2021 in a pilot programme — or buprenorphine) and naloxone for overdose. Treatment settings include drug rehabilitation units in neuropsychiatric hospitals, NDLEA centres and NGOs; harm reduction (needle and syringe programmes) reduces HIV transmission among people who inject drugs.

topics.title: Child, Adolescent and Organic Psychiatry
topics.summary: ADHD, autism, intellectual disability, delirium and dementia, and epilepsy-related psychiatric problems.

material.heading: Child and adolescent
material.body: Neurodevelopmental disorders: intellectual disability (IQ < 70 with deficits in adaptive functioning; causes include birth asphyxia, kernicterus, infections, malnutrition, iodine deficiency, Down syndrome and fragile X), autism spectrum disorder (persistent deficits in social communication and restricted, repetitive behaviours from early childhood; early intervention — behavioural and communication therapies; awareness is growing in Nigeria), and ADHD (inattention, hyperactivity and impulsivity in more than one setting before age 12; parent training, school support and stimulants like methylphenidate). Adolescents face depression, anxiety, substance use, self-harm, conduct problems and eating disorders; confidentiality and involvement of family and school are balanced. Child abuse, 'almajiri' deprivation, bullying and exam stress affect mental health. School mental health programmes promote early detection.

material.heading: Organic psychiatry
material.body: Delirium is an acute, fluctuating disturbance of attention and awareness with disorganised thinking, caused by a medical condition (infection — malaria, sepsis, pneumonia, UTI; drugs; alcohol or sedative withdrawal; hypoxia; metabolic — hypoglycaemia, electrolyte and renal/hepatic failure; post-operative). It is common in the elderly and in hospital; hypoactive delirium is easily missed. Management: identify and treat the cause, reorientation, family presence, good lighting, avoid restraints and unnecessary sedation (low-dose haloperidol for severe agitation). Dementia is chronic progressive cognitive decline impairing daily function — Alzheimer's disease (commonest), vascular dementia (stroke, hypertension), HIV-associated neurocognitive disorder, and others; screen with MMSE or culturally adapted tools (e.g. the Community Screening Interview for Dementia used in Ibadan studies); exclude reversible causes (B12, thyroid, syphilis, depression — 'pseudodementia'); support carers. Epilepsy is associated with depression, psychosis and stigma.
